quote: Was ist [-fester z.B.-] fester Körper, Flüssigkeit, Gas, Aether, Elek- tricität etc unter der Annahme der Molekulartheorie.
english: What are a solid body, liquid, gas, aether, electricity etc. under the assumption of molecular theory?
topic: The page discusses how hard it is to prove that a differential equation cannot be solved by a single quadrature, then asks how solids, liquids, gases, aether and electricity should be described under molecular theory using mean values and expansions in small parameters, and finally states that the function zeta(s,x) = sum x^n/n^s satisfies no known differential equation.

triage.modern_statement: This is a programme question, not a single theorem. It asks how continuum descriptions of matter (solids, liquids, gases) and of the aether and electricity can be derived from an underlying molecular or atomistic model. The page context points to the method: take mean values and expand in small parameters. In modern terms this is the rigorous derivation of macroscopic continuum equations from microscopic particle dynamics. For gases, for example, one goes from Newtonian hard-sphere dynamics to the Boltzmann equation (Boltzmann–Grad limit), then on to the compressible Euler and Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations (hydrodynamic limit). Hilbert later put this into the second part of his 6th Problem (1900), which asks for the limiting processes 'which lead from the atomistic view to the laws of motion of continua'. The note's 'aether' and 'electricity' parts are dated physics and have no precise modern mathematical counterpart.
triage.answered_by: This is not a single solved problem. It is a forerunner of the atomistic-to-continuum part of Hilbert's 6th Problem. The most notable recent progress is for gases: in 2025 Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma (arXiv:2503.01800) rigorously derived the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations from hard-sphere Newtonian dynamics via Boltzmann's kinetic theory. Their claim to have resolved the gas case has been disputed, and the general programme (solids, dense liquids, all density regimes, quantum versions) is widely seen as still open. L. Saint-Raymond and co-authors and the 2018 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A theme issue (ed. A. N. Gorban) are other relevant work.

evidence.claim: In his explanation of the 6th Problem, Hilbert asked for the limiting processes that lead from the atomistic view to the laws of motion of continua, alongside probability.
Deng, Hani and Ma (2025) present a derivation of the fluid equations from Newton's laws by way of Boltzmann's kinetic theory, framed as Hilbert's sixth problem.

A critical response argues that Deng–Hani–Ma advance only a narrow, dilute-gas front. It says the Sixth Problem stays open in general, needing a kinetic theory for all density regimes and direct particle-to-fluid derivations.

Saint-Raymond and co-authors are developing an approach from the atomistic view to the continuum laws that skips the intermediate kinetic equations. The sixth problem has inspired several waves of research.
A 2018 Royal Society theme issue on Hilbert's sixth problem covers related work, such as Golse on semiclassical mean-field limits of the quantum N-body problem.

triage.why: The note asks what states of matter are under molecular theory, and the page talks about mean values and small-parameter expansions. That is the atomistic-to-continuum question Hilbert later made public as part of his 6th Problem. Calling it a published problem is my reading of how well the topics match; I found no source that discusses this diary entry itself. The gas case has seen major recent progress (Deng–Hani–Ma 2025), though whether it is fully resolved is disputed. The broad programme is still open and actively researched. Confidence is medium because the note is vague and includes outdated physics (aether, electricity as a substance), so no single precise theorem can be pinned to it.
